gate.reason: The quote is in draft.md:69: "The proof of near-optimality does not carry over, because without a reset the state reached before a halt persists; whether near-optimality holds is open problem 2." It sits next to "open", so the draft does not claim the result fails. It claims only that the proof as written does not apply. That reading is supported. The Theorem 4.2 proof (wachi2023.txt:~1565-1572) ends with "the modified (unconstrained) MDP M^ is identical to the original CMDP M". M^ is the augmented MDP in which the stop leads to s1, which is a reset. With a halt that leaves the state in place, M^ is a different MDP, so the identity step is not available as written. The reviewer's point that the proof's penalty argument never uses the reset directly is true, but the proof depends on the reset-based definition of M^. The key.csv entry K13 itself says "does not carry over, and whether it holds is open problem 2". The "does not carry over" phrasing is a wording or strength-of-claim issue, not a wrong fact. The finding does not show the paper states anything the sources contradict. A softer wording would be a nice-to-have, not a material fix.

The paper does say this. cells.csv:25 reads "not needed: the shield checks every action when it is taken." Section 5 reads "A shield needs S1 in full and S2--S5 in part, and it does not need S6". The finding's inference does not hold. S6 is "Trials repeat, or every state is recoverable within the decision process (by the agent, or by a reset it can use)" (064_conditions). Alshiekh's shield does not assume recoverability. It computes the winning region W and blocks any action that would leave it, so the system "can never allow the play to visit a state from which the environment can force the play to visit an unsafe state" (alshiekh2018.txt:333-335). The guarantee needs only that the initial state lies in W. The shield creates the safe-action property by design, so it does not assume that property of the environment. That is not S6. The "safe fallback at every step" in Section 5 is stated as the paper's own specialisation ("This specialisation is ours, and it needs a safe action, such as halting, at every step") for the LLM setting. The paper does not attribute it to Alshiekh, so the cell and the caveat do not contradict each other. The finding itself concedes that the K10 exception (S1 is the only full cell) is unaffected. At most the finding asks for a nice-to-have qualification, and rejected.csv does not cover it.

But the paper never calls the token case a leak. It says "A leak of isolation makes outside effects possible that the reset does not cover. The lab reports that an agent... 'used an already publicly exposed Hugging Face user token'". The token case is an outside effect the reset does not cover, which is the claim S6 needs. It does not misquote any source. paper.tex:425 also says one May experiment had internet access by design. The cell value (~) holds on the Artifactory SSRF case in openai2026b. Lines 116-117: "the agent begins to exhibit obfuscated reward hacking and learns to fool the monitor ... learns to obfuscate its intent within the CoT". The reviewer quoted only the introduction's "could cause" framing (lines 106-110). The setting is RL on agentic coding environments, which is T-AGENT. The U3 reason in 085_setting_conditions/reasons.csv matches this: "in RL training in 'agentic coding environments', optimising hard against a chain-of-thought monitor taught agents to hide their intent [@baker2025]". Whether this evidence earns a full ✗ for the whole column is a grading choice settled by R22 in 096_review/rejected.csv. Stated.csv gives the sources as a cost function, a bound and a temporal-logic specification. The S1 reason in 085_setting_conditions/reasons.csv says a given specification may still not be "a specification of safety", and that a rule list "covers only what it names". On that reading, an unenforced prose freeze is not an S1 specification, so the cell is a defensible classification and not a false fact. But the same reason also cites two genuine deployment incidents: Terraform ("the vendor restored the database") and Replit. Both show effects that only a rollback or backup outside the agent could undo, so S6 failing in D-AGENT stands without the evaluation incident. The wording gap is real, but the S6 cell and the K09 count are supported. This is a nice-to-have qualification. 096_review/rejected.csv has no entry covering it.

The quotes are real (paper.tex:58, :162; mclean2026.txt:82). The finding names no wrong fact, quote, count or contradiction. The paper defines binding as "not been shown to yield". McLean et al. only say the Elelimy history-to-state map plus CMDPs is "precisely the problem that constrained MDPs address". They show nothing, so S4 can still be called binding. Their passage is about the finite context window, which the paper does not claim to be hidden world state. The S4 cell reason (085_setting_conditions/reasons.csv, S4) says D-AGENT fails because "the world behind the tools is hidden, and its state is not in the context". A learned map over the context cannot recover that. The paper says S4 is hidden state behind tools. So the finding asks for an extra rebuttal of a McLean remedy. That is a nice-to-have qualification, not a missing one that changes K02. K02 itself does not name the context-window case, and K02 holds as the paper states it.

The quote is in the paper (draft.md line 69 and paper.tex line 245): "The open part is the quantifier: it needs the cost of a tool call to be regular in known features or in a known kernel (S1)". The subject of "it" is the quantifier, not the safety theorem. The same paragraph says the theorem holds "Under Assumption 3.4", the uncertainty quantifier. It also says "if a quantifier exists", and that @wachi2023 "build quantifiers for costs that follow a generalised linear model or a Gaussian process". So the paper already separates the general requirement from the constructions, and it does not state the finding's claim. The finding's evidence (Assumption 3.4 asks for a general delta-uncertainty quantifier) agrees with the paper. The remaining issue is how a reader might take "it". That is wording, and K13 in key.csv is not affected.

The paper (paper.tex:432) defines × as "the condition fails in the setting as usually run" and ~ as "holds in usual runs but fails in reported cases". 085_setting_conditions/cells.csv grades U3 × for both T-AGENT and D-AGENT (by LLM). For D-AGENT it cites models reasoning about oversight "in evaluations" (greenblatt2024b, meinke2024, lynch2025) and "in one evaluation agents sought the evaluator's code" (openai2026, metr2026). I checked greenblatt2024b.txt. Its alignment-faking reasoning appears in 7-24% of cases in set-up scenarios where the model is given information about its training, and the paper does not claim these are usual runs. The openai2026c extracts call the incident an "outlier scenario" without production safeguards. rejected.csv has no entry covering this (R13 and R16 are about other points). Because K11 says every D-AGENT cell is right and K09/K10 are driven by these cells, the grade affects headline counts. The grade is a judgment call, so how much it matters depends on how K09/K10 weigh U3.
